implementation_notes: TypeScript compiles to JavaScript, so the JavaScript wins apply unchanged - shape stability, allocation, property-access hoisting, typed arrays - and the type system's contribution is preventing two of them structurally: a union-typed or any-typed value at a hot site is a megamorphic access that cannot be inlined (narrow it with a discriminant or a type guard so the site becomes monomorphic), and generics force the monomorphic shape the JIT wants. TypeScript adds no runtime performance of its own, so the profiling is V8's (--cpu-prof, Chrome DevTools Performance, --trace-gc), and the discipline is identical. The honest answer for anything CPU-heavy in TypeScript is the same as JavaScript: this is not the language to micro-optimise arithmetic in - move the work to typed arrays, a worker, or native/WASM.
idiom_name: V8 --cpu-prof / Chrome Performance attribution; TypeScript's contribution is keeping hot sites monomorphic by construction (no unions/any on the hot path)
pitfalls: A union-typed or any-typed value on a hot path is a megamorphic access that defeats the inline cache; narrow it with a discriminated union or a type guard.
Generic TypeScript compiles away entirely (types are erased), so a generic gives no monomorphism benefit the way a Rust or Swift generic does - only a union/any is a runtime hazard.
node --trace-gc shows whether GC, not computation, is the real cost.
V8 tiers its optimisation: a cold one-shot run measures the interpreter, so warm up before measuring.
Micro-optimising TypeScript arithmetic is usually the wrong investment; move the work to typed arrays, a Worker or WASM.
